title: Imports and Dependencies
content: Imports Mathlib's SimpleGraph for graph structure, Nat.Log for the natural number logarithm function used in the bounds, Real.Basic for real number support, and general tactics. The Nat.log function is essential for expressing the bounds $\lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor$.
mathContext: Uses $\text{Nat.log}\,2\,n = \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor$ for the binary logarithm.

title: Pancyclic Graph
content: A graph on $n$ vertices is pancyclic if it contains cycles of every length $k$ for $3 \leq k \leq n$. This is a much stronger property than being Hamiltonian (which only requires a cycle of length $n$). The definition is parameterized by the edge count and a predicate hasCycleOfLength, abstracting away the graph structure. Pancyclicity was introduced by Bondy (1971) who showed that Ore's condition for Hamiltonicity also implies pancyclicity (or bipartiteness).
mathContext: $G$ is pancyclic iff $\forall k \in \{3, 4, \ldots, n\},\, C_k \subseteq G$.

title: Pancyclic Excess h(n)
content: The pancyclic excess $h(n)$ is the minimum number of edges beyond $n$ required for an $n$-vertex graph to be pancyclic: $h(n) = \min\{|E(G)| - n : G$ is pancyclic on $n$ vertices$\}$. Since a Hamiltonian cycle uses exactly $n$ edges, $h(n)$ measures how many additional edges are needed to ensure all shorter cycle lengths exist. The function is defined as a supremum of lower bounds on edge count.

title: Iterated Logarithm log*
content: The iterated logarithm $\log^* n$ counts how many times the binary logarithm must be applied to $n$ before the result is $\leq 1$. It grows extraordinarily slowly: $\log^*(2^{65536}) = 5$. This function appears in the upper bound for $h(n)$ and represents the subtle correction beyond the main $\log_2 n$ term. The recursive definition handles base cases $0$ and $1$ (returning $0$) and recursively applies $\text{Nat.log}\,2$.

title: Main Conjecture: h(n) >= log_2 n + log* n - O(1)
content: Erdos conjectured that the lower bound for $h(n)$ matches the George-Khodkar-Wallis upper bound up to a constant: $h(n) \geq \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor + \log^* n - C$ for some absolute constant $C$. Combined with the upper bound $h(n) \leq \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor + \log^* n + O(1)$, this would pinpoint $h(n) = \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor + \log^* n + \Theta(1)$, giving an asymptotic formula with only a bounded additive error.
mathContext: $\exists C,\, \forall n \geq 3: h(n) + C \geq \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor + \log^* n$.

title: Weaker Open Question: h(n) - log_2 n -> infinity
content: Even the weaker statement that $h(n) - \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor \to \infty$ is open. Erdos noted he could not prove this despite believing the stronger conjecture. This would show that the excess grows strictly faster than $\log_2 n$, without specifying the rate. The formalization expresses this as: for any $M$, eventually $h(n) \geq \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor + M$.
mathContext: $\forall M,\, \exists N,\, \forall n \geq N: h(n) \geq \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor + M$.
relatedConcepts: open problems in extremal graph theory

title: Bondy's Lower Bound (Griffin 2013)
content: The lower bound $h(n) \geq \lfloor \log_2(n-1) \rfloor - 1$ was conjectured by Bondy in 1971 but the first published proof was by Griffin in 2013. The proof uses a counting argument: a pancyclic graph must contain cycles of $n-2$ different lengths, and each additional edge beyond the Hamiltonian cycle can create at most a bounded number of new cycle lengths, requiring at least logarithmically many extra edges.

title: George-Khodkar-Wallis Upper Bound (2016)
content: George, Khodkar, and Wallis proved that $h(n) \leq \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor + \log^* n + O(1)$ by constructing explicit pancyclic graphs on $n$ vertices with this many edges beyond $n$. Their construction uses a hierarchical structure: a Hamiltonian cycle plus carefully placed chords that create cycles of all intermediate lengths. The $\log^* n$ term arises from the tower-like structure needed to cover all cycle lengths efficiently.
mathContext: $\exists C,\, \forall n \geq 3: h(n) \leq \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor + \log^* n + C$.

title: Hamiltonian Edge Count Baseline
content: A Hamiltonian cycle on $n$ vertices uses exactly $n$ edges. Since every pancyclic graph must contain a Hamiltonian cycle (the cycle of length $n$), the pancyclic excess $h(n) \geq 0$ is guaranteed. The excess measures how many additional edges beyond this Hamiltonian cycle baseline are needed.

title: Bondy's Quadratic Threshold
content: Bondy (1971) proved that any graph with at least $n^2/4$ edges is either pancyclic or bipartite (the Turan graph $T(n,2)$ is the extremal bipartite example). This gives a sufficient condition for pancyclicity but is far from tight: $n^2/4 \gg n + \log n$ for large $n$. The precise edge threshold for pancyclicity is exactly $n + h(n)$, which is only logarithmically above $n$.
mathContext: $|E(G)| \geq n^2/4 \Rightarrow G$ is pancyclic or bipartite. But $n^2/4 \gg n + \log_2 n$.

title: Monotonicity of Pancyclicity
content: Pancyclicity is a monotone graph property: adding edges to a pancyclic graph preserves pancyclicity, since the existing cycles remain present. This means the set of pancyclic graphs on $n$ vertices forms an upward-closed family in the edge-ordering.
mathContext: If $G$ is pancyclic and $G \subseteq G'$ (same vertices, $E(G) \subseteq E(G')$), then $G'$ is pancyclic.

title: Small Cases: h(3) = 0, h(4) = 1
content: The triangle $K_3$ is pancyclic on 3 vertices with exactly 3 edges, giving $h(3) = 0$. For $n = 4$, a pancyclic graph needs cycles of lengths 3 and 4; a 4-cycle with one diagonal (5 edges = 4 + 1) suffices, so $h(4) = 1$. Further values are catalogued in OEIS A105206.

title: Tightness of Known Bounds
content: The gap between the known lower bound $\lfloor \log_2(n-1) \rfloor - 1$ and upper bound $\lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor + \log^* n + O(1)$ is at most $\log^* n + O(1)$, an incredibly slowly growing function. This makes Erdos Problem #1016 one of the tightest open problems in extremal graph theory: the answer is known to within an additive $\log^* n$ term.
